question.question:
D1 — Build the retry scheduler inline, or use the job library's retry hooks with a custom backoff curve?
Project/branch/task: main — reviewing PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework"; the plan proposes a hand-rolled exponential-backoff scheduler inside each of 5 workers.
ELI10: The job library already knows how to retry a failed job: it stores the attempt count, waits, and re-runs it, and almost every mainstream library lets you plug in your own delay formula. The plan rebuilds that machinery inside each worker so "we control the curve." That control is already available through the library's backoff callback, and the rebuilt version has to re-solve persistence, visibility and crash safety on its own.
Stakes if we pick wrong: an in-process retry timer dies with the worker, so a crash or deploy mid-backoff silently drops the job; retry counts and dead-letter state vanish from the library's dashboards and tooling.
Recommendation: A because the library's hook gives the same curve control with persistence and tooling for free [Layer 1]; rebuilding it is accidental complexity in 5 places.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=4/10, C=n/a (bounded investigation, decides nothing)
Pros / cons:
A) Library retry hooks + custom backoff callback (recommended)
  ✅ Retry state (attempt count, next-run time, dead-letter) persists in the queue store and survives worker crashes and deploys
  ✅ Existing library tooling (dashboards, admin retry, metrics) keeps working; one backoff function instead of five schedulers (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ❌ Curve is bounded by the hook's inputs (often attempt number only), so error-specific delays like Retry-After need a small wrapper
B) Custom inline scheduler in each worker (plan as written)
  ✅ Unlimited control over delay math and per-error behavior without touching library config
  ✅ No dependency on the library's backoff API shape or version
  ❌ Retries live in worker memory unless you also build persistence; a crash during backoff loses the job silently and bypasses the library's retry visibility (human: ~1 week / CC: ~1 hr, plus 5 copies to maintain)
C) Investigate first: bounded probe of the library's backoff hook
  ✅ Confirms whether the installed library's hook supports the exact curve before committing either way
  ✅ Cheap: read the library docs and one worker's current retry config (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
  ❌ Decides nothing; R1 stays pending and Sections 1–4 proceed against the plan as written
Net: trading a bounded callback signature for crash-safe, observable retries you don't have to write five times.

question.question:
D2 — What delivery guarantee does the retried processWebhookJob keep, and what regression test proves it?
Project/branch/task: main — reviewing PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework"; the webhook job is rewritten under the new retry path and currently guarantees at-most-once delivery.
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent once; if it fails, it is gone. Adding retries means the same event can be sent again. Sometimes the first send actually arrived but the response got lost, so the retry delivers a duplicate. Receivers that bill, email or create records on each webhook will double-act unless we give them a way to recognise a repeat.
Stakes if we pick wrong: downstream systems process duplicate events (double charges, double notifications) with no test telling us the guarantee changed, or webhook failures stay unrecovered forever.
Recommendation: A because it recovers failed sends and keeps receivers safe from duplicates, and the four assertions make the guarantee executable rather than implied.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=5/10, C=6/10
Pros / cons:
A) Idempotent retried delivery (recommended)
  ✅ Failed webhooks are retried, and a stable per-job idempotency-key header plus a persisted delivered marker let receivers and the worker dedup repeats
  ✅ Four concrete assertions cover first-try success, 5xx-then-2xx, lost response and lost ack, so the regression test fails on any semantic slip (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ❌ Receivers must honor the idempotency header to be fully safe; the marker adds one persisted field per job
B) Explicit at-least-once
  ✅ Simplest code: library retry with no key or marker; one changelog note documents the new semantics
  ✅ Still recovers failed webhooks that were previously dropped
  ❌ Duplicates reach receivers on every ambiguous outcome, and the only test is "a 5xx schedules a retry"
C) Exclude webhooks from retry
  ✅ Preserves the exact current at-most-once guarantee with a one-assertion regression test
  ✅ Zero risk of duplicate side effects downstream
  ❌ Webhook failures stay unrecovered, which is the problem this plan set out to fix; the webhook rewrite then has no purpose
Net: trading one header and one persisted flag for retries that cannot double-act on receivers.

options.label: Idempotent retried delivery (recommended)
options.description: Retry failed webhook POSTs via the library hooks (D1), send a stable per-job idempotency-key header on every attempt, and persist a delivered marker on 2xx that is checked before each attempt. Regression contract: (1) 2xx on attempt 1 → exactly one POST, no retry; (2) 5xx then 2xx → two POSTs with identical key; (3) send succeeds, response times out → retry carries the same key; (4) marker set but ack lost → no second POST. ✅ Recovers failed sends and dedups repeats. ✅ Guarantee is executable, not implied (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min). ❌ Receivers must honor the header; one persisted field per job. question.question:
D3 — Should retry delays be randomized (jitter), and how?
Project/branch/task: main — reviewing PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework"; the backoff callback approved in D1 needs its curve defined, starting with jitter.
ELI10: When a downstream service goes down, every job that failed at the same moment computes the same retry delay and comes back at the same moment, so the recovering service gets hit by a wave and falls over again. Jitter adds randomness to each delay so retries spread out. Full jitter picks any delay from zero up to the computed value; equal jitter keeps half the delay fixed and randomizes the other half.
Stakes if we pick wrong: synchronized retry storms after every outage, or (with equal jitter) a longer mandatory floor than needed.
Recommendation: A because full jitter spreads load best for the same code size [Layer 1]; the only cost is that a retry can occasionally fire almost immediately.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=8/10, C=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full jitter (recommended)
  ✅ Spreads retries across the whole window, so a recovering service sees a trickle instead of a wave (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~5 min incl. seeded test)
  ✅ Same one-line callback as the plain curve; well documented standard practice
  ❌ A retry may fire almost immediately after failure, which wastes one attempt when the outage is still ongoing
B) Equal jitter
  ✅ Guarantees a minimum wait of half the computed delay, so no near-instant retry
  ✅ Still breaks synchronization across jobs
  ❌ Slightly more contention than full jitter and a larger mandatory floor at high attempt counts
C) No jitter
  ✅ Fully deterministic delays are easy to reason about and test exactly
  ✅ Zero extra code
  ❌ Every job that failed together retries together; the thundering-herd failure mode is left open
Net: trading exact predictability of one delay for a recovering dependency that is not re-flattened by our own retries.

options.label: Full jitter (recommended)
options.description: Backoff callback returns random(0, base × 2^attempt). Unit test with seeded RNG: delay within [0, formula]; two jobs at the same attempt get different delays. ✅ Spreads retries across the whole window (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~5 min). ✅ One-line callback, standard practice. ❌ A retry may fire almost immediately. Completeness 9/10. R7, R8 pending (cap applies pre-jitter when decided); R2, R4, R9 pending.

options.label: Equal jitter
options.description: Callback returns half the formula plus random(0, half). Unit test: delay within [half, full]; two jobs differ. ✅ Guaranteed minimum wait. ✅ Still desynchronizes. ❌ More contention than full jitter and a larger floor at high attempts. Completeness 8/10. R7, R8, R2, R4, R9 pending.

options.label: No jitter
options.description: Callback returns base × 2^attempt exactly. Unit test: exact values per attempt. ✅ Deterministic and exact. ✅ Zero extra code. ❌ Thundering herd after outages stays open. Completeness 4/10. R7, R8, R2, R4, R9 pending.

# Plan: Add background job retry framework

We'll roll a custom exponential-backoff scheduler inline in each worker

shape as the library version, but we want full control over the curve.

Completeness: A=9/10, B=8/10, C=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full jitter (recommended)
  ✅ Spreads retries across the whole window, so a recovering service sees a trickle instead of a wave (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~5 min incl. seeded test)
  ✅ Same one-line callback as the plain curve; well documented standard practice
  ❌ A retry may fire almost immediately after failure, which wastes one attempt when the outage is still ongoing
B) Equal jitter
  ✅ Guarantees a minimum wait of half the computed delay, so no near-instant retry
  ✅ Still breaks synchronization across jobs
  ❌ Slightly more contention than full jitter and a larger mandatory floor at high attempt counts
C) No jitter
  ✅ Fully deterministic delays are easy to reason about and test exactly
  ✅ Zero extra code
  ❌ Every job that failed together retries together; the thundering-herd failure mode is left open
Net: trading exact predictability of one delay for a recovering dependency that is not re-flattened by our own retries.
